summary.text: The proof evaluates the relevant initial primorials, counts the qualifying divisors at each proposed candidate, and exhaustively shows that every smaller modulus has a different count. For the largest search it uses, for each positive divisor \(d\mid k\), the equivalence \(d^d\equiv d\pmod{k}\iff d^{d-1}\equiv1\pmod{k/d}\), making the finite exclusion of all smaller moduli tractable.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(n)=\#\{d:d\mid n,\ d^d\equiv d\pmod n\}.
\]
Here divisors are positive divisors. At \(n=0\) we use the convention that the finite divisor list is empty, so \(F(0)=0\). Define
\[
a(r)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N:F(k)=r\};
\]
the minima needed below exist because in each case we exhibit an appropriate \(k\).

We shall prove
\[
a(1)=1,\quad a(2)=2,\quad a(3)=6,\quad a(6)=30,
\quad a(7)=210,\quad a(10)=2310.
\]
Afterward, identifying these six integers with the corresponding primorials will give the asserted statement.

First we derive the congruence test used in all the finite calculations. Suppose that \(d>0\) and \(d\mid n\), and put
\[
m=\frac nd.
\]
Thus \(n=md\). Since \(d>0\),
\[
d^d=d^{d-1}d.
\]
Reduction modulo \(md\), together with the elementary identity
\[
(xd)\bmod(md)=((x\bmod m)d),
\]
gives
\[
d^d\bmod n=((d^{d-1}\bmod m)d),
\qquad
d\bmod n=((1\bmod m)d).
\]
Consequently these two remainders are equal if and only if
\[
d^{d-1}\bmod m=1\bmod m,
\]
because one may cancel the positive integer \(d\) from an equality of ordinary natural numbers. Powers may themselves be reduced modulo \(m\), so the test can be written as
\[
\boxed{
 d^d\equiv d\pmod n
 \iff
 ((d\bmod (n/d))^{d-1})\bmod(n/d)=1\bmod(n/d).
}
\tag{1}
\]
This also handles the divisor \(d=n\), for which \(n/d=1\): both sides of the last remainder equality are then zero.

Thus, for positive \(n\), \(F(n)\) can be found by listing the divisors \(d\) of \(n\), setting \(m=n/d\), and applying (1). This criterion avoids forming the usually enormous integer \(d^d\).

We first evaluate \(F\) at the six proposed minima. The complete divisor lists and the sublists that pass criterion (1) are as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{c|l|l|c}
n&\text{all positive divisors of }n&
\text{divisors satisfying }d^d\equiv d\pmod n&F(n)\\ \hline
1&1&1&1\\
2&1,2&1,2&2\\
6&1,2,3,6&1,3,6&3\\
30&1,2,3,5,6,10,15,30&1,5,6,10,15,30&6\\
210&1,2,3,5,6,7,10,14,15,21,30,35,42,70,105,210&
1,15,21,35,70,105,210&7\\
2310&
\begin{array}{l}
1,2,3,5,6,7,10,11,14,15,21,22,30,33,35,42,55,66,\\
70,77,105,110,154,165,210,231,330,385,462,770,1155,2310
\end{array}
&
1,21,55,77,210,231,330,385,1155,2310&10
\end{array}
\]

For clarity, every entry in the third column is obtained by the same elementary modular procedure: for each divisor \(d\) in the second column, compute \(m=n/d\), start with \(1\bmod m\), multiply by \(d\bmod m\) a total of \(d-1\) times, reducing modulo \(m\) after each multiplication, and retain \(d\) precisely when the resulting residue is \(1\bmod m\). Criterion (1) proves that this is exactly the original condition. The displayed complete divisor lists also show that no divisor was omitted. Their cardinalities therefore establish
\[
F(1)=1,
\quad F(2)=2,
\quad F(6)=3,
\quad F(30)=6,
\quad F(210)=7,
\quad F(2310)=10.
\tag{2}
\]

It remains to prove minimality. This is a finite question in each case. We describe the exhaustive calculation precisely. For every integer \(k\) in a stated interval, its divisor list was formed by retaining, among \(1,\ldots,k\), exactly those \(d\) for which the remainder of \(k\) on division by \(d\) is zero. For every retained \(d\), criterion (1) was evaluated by successive modular multiplication as just described. The passing divisors were counted. The following table records the complete ranges tested and the result relevant to the proof:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{desired count }r&\text{range of }k&\text{result}\\ \hline
1&\{0\}&F(k)\ne1\\
2&\{0,1\}&F(k)\ne2\\
3&0\le k<6&F(k)\ne3\\
6&0\le k<10&F(k)\ne6\\
 &10\le k<20&F(k)\ne6\\
 &20\le k<30&F(k)\ne6\\
7&0\le k<70&F(k)\ne7\\
 &70\le k<140&F(k)\ne7\\
 &140\le k<210&F(k)\ne7\\
10&0\le k<1&F(k)\ne10\\
 &1\le k<300&F(k)\ne10\\
 &300\le k<600&F(k)\ne10\\
 &600\le k<900&F(k)\ne10\\
 &900\le k<1200&F(k)\ne10\\
 &1200\le k<1500&F(k)\ne10\\
 &1500\le k<1800&F(k)\ne10\\
 &1800\le k<2100&F(k)\ne10\\
 &2100\le k<2310&F(k)\ne10
\end{array}
\tag{3}
\]

These are exhaustive finite searches, not probabilistic tests: the intervals in each block are consecutive, disjoint, and their union is exactly the set of natural numbers below the proposed minimum. Each individual test consists only of trial division and modular multiplication governed by the proved equivalence (1). For the first two rows one can also see the result immediately: by convention \(F(0)=0\), while the first row of (2) gives \(F(1)=1\).

Combining (2) and (3), we obtain:

* \(F(1)=1\), whereas no \(k<1\) has value \(1\), so \(a(1)=1\).
* \(F(2)=2\), whereas no \(k<2\) has value \(2\), so \(a(2)=2\).
* \(F(6)=3\), whereas no \(k<6\) has value \(3\), so \(a(3)=6\).
* \(F(30)=6\), whereas no \(k<30\) has value \(6\), so \(a(6)=30\).
* \(F(210)=7\), whereas no \(k<210\) has value \(7\), so \(a(7)=210\).
* \(F(2310)=10\), whereas no \(k<2310\) has value \(10\), so \(a(10)=2310\).

This use of minimality is justified directly by the well-ordering of \(\mathbb N\): if \(F(m)=r\) and \(F(k)\ne r\) for all \(k<m\), then \(m\) is the least member of \(\{k:F(k)=r\}\), hence is its infimum and equals \(a(r)\).

Finally we identify the right-hand sides with the primorial sequence. The primes in increasing order begin
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,\ldots.
\]
Indeed, \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) are prime; after \(3\), the only intervening integer before \(5\) is \(4=2^2\); after \(5\), \(6=2\cdot3\); after \(7\), the intervening integers are \(8=2^3\), \(9=3^2\), and \(10=2\cdot5\); and after \(11\), \(12=2^2\cdot3\). Thus there are no omitted primes in these gaps.

By definition, \(A002110(0)=1\), and for positive \(j\), \(A002110(j)\) is the product of the first \(j\) primes. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
A002110(0)&=1,\\
A002110(1)&=2,\\
A002110(2)&=2\cdot3=6,\\
A002110(3)&=2\cdot3\cdot5=30,\\
A002110(4)&=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210,\\
A002110(5)&=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution into the six minimality conclusions proves
\[
a(1)=A002110(0),\quad
a(2)=A002110(1),\quad
a(3)=A002110(2),\quad
a(6)=A002110(3),\quad
a(7)=A002110(4),\quad
a(10)=A002110(5),
\]
as required.
